feature.name: Pricing Change
feature.description:
current pricing tiers are 0$(limited use case) and 20$(full access)
which we are not changing to 20$(full access with limits on total discounts) and 50$(full access + no limits)

verdictRationale: PersonaFleet is available and recommends iterate: it shows a polarized response, low satisfaction with the new pricing (mean 31.4), and the $20 discount cap as the dominant blocker, while the $50 unlimited tier has support from high-volume/BFCM personas. Financial recommends proceed_with_caution because the change is low-cost and within the $10k threshold, but market evidence is thin and regression is skipped. Therefore finalVerdict aligns with iterate: refine pricing/cap and test before broad rollout rather than ship or do_not_ship.
executiveSummary: Fly Upsell & Cross Sell should iterate on the proposed pricing change. Regression evidence is skipped, so no test signal exists. Market evidence is available but thin: competitor pricing clusters around $15–$60, usage caps exist, and BFCM capacity is marketed, yet the $20 cap is the main churn vector against a ~1,125 merchant base with short retention. Persona fleet is polarized: the $50 unlimited tier appeals to high-volume promo merchants, but the capped $20 tier is widely seen as a downgrade; satisfaction is 31.4 and recommendation likelihood is 43.1. Financial impact is small—1 engineer at 20% and support at 20% within $10k—but proceed_with_caution. Overall: iterate on cap design, grandfathering/retention, and staged BFCM rollout before broad launch.

market.summary: Market evidence is available from Strategy C but limited. Competitor list prices cluster roughly $15–$60/month; usage-capped monetization already exists; BFCM capacity is a marketing battleground. The new $50 tier sits at the top of the observed band and the recapped $20 tier sits near entry pricing. Internal ARPU is $8/merchant/month with $9k MRR (~1,125 merchants), so $20→$50 upgrades add $30/month. The $20 cap is the main churn vector, especially for low-change and small-scale personas.
highlights: Kaching Bundles publicly lists Free to install, $14.99, $29.99, $59.99 per month; a Shopify blog describes Kaching paid plans from ~$15 Starter and ~$30 Scale.
Rapi Bundles Pro plan covers up to $10,000 of extra usage, indicating usage-capped competitors exist.
Rebolt and Adsgun market BFCM/seasonal readiness; the BFCM Campaign Power User upgrade trigger matches this need.
Current revenue is $8 per merchant per month and MRR is $9,000 (implied ~1,125 merchants); each $20→$50 upgrade adds $30/month.
risks: The capped $20 tier reduces prior full-access value at the same price, creating churn/downgrade risk for Efficient Small-Scale Merchant and Stable, Low-Change Merchant personas.
Competitor entry prices are lower (~$14.99–$15/month), so merchants hitting the cap may substitute rather than upgrade to $50.
Retention is 4 months with $40 average LTV and $4 CAC, so pricing friction must be net accretive within roughly four months.
Competitor intelligence is unverified: company_enrich calls for Rapi Bundles, Fast Bundles, and Kaching Bundles failed, and target-market company_search returned mostly agencies/app vendors.
No internal upgrade, churn, plan-mix, or discount-usage data was provided.

personaFleet.summary: Persona fleet recommends iterate. The response is polarized: the $50 unlimited tier is compelling for high-volume BFCM/promotional personas (upgrade means 90.4 and 88.3), while the capped $20 tier is widely perceived as a downgrade/repackaging and is rejected by low-volume/stable personas. Fleet composite mean 46.5, median 48.6, satisfaction with new pricing mean 31.4, and recommendation likelihood mean 43.1. The $20 discount cap is the dominant blocker (approxCount 25).
highlights: The $50 unlimited plan addresses a real need: importanceOfUnlimitedDiscounts mean 57.4 and median 93, with 13 of 25 agents scoring 80–100.
High-volume BFCM and promotional merchants show upgrade intent: upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited means are 90.4 for persona_1 and 88.3 for persona_2.
The $20 capped plan retains low-volume merchants: continueOnTwentyWithLimits means are 86.2 for persona_3 and 73.2 for new_install.
The $20 plan discount limits/caps are a negative theme with approxCount 25; pricing feels like a hike/repackaging with approxCount 24.
Satisfaction with the new pricing is low (mean 31.4), and the response is structurally polarized, with upgrade intent split between 0–19 and 80–100.

financial.summary: Financial recommends proceed_with_caution. The change is low-cost: 1 engineer at 20% occupancy for one week and support at 20% occupancy, within the $10k threshold. Company health shows 18 months runway, $9k MRR, 70% margins, $0 burn, $4 CAC, 4-month retention, and $40 average LTV. CFO workspace is connected but scenario, memory, page, and integration calls returned validation errors; only an uploaded report reference is available. Market/persona polarization and low satisfaction are the main cautions.
highlights: Investment is within the $10k threshold: 1 engineer at 20% occupancy for one week and support at 20% occupancy.
Runway is 18 months with $9k MRR, 70% margins, $0 burn, $4 CAC, 4-month retention, and $40 average LTV.
The $50 unlimited tier has strong appeal for high-volume BFCM/promotional merchants.
Low-cost, short-duration change enables testing before broad rollout.

crossCuttingThemes: $20 discount cap is the primary negative theme and churn vector.
Pricing change is perceived by some as a hike/repackaging of prior $20 full access.
High-volume BFCM/promotional merchants show $50 unlimited upgrade interest.
Low-volume/stable merchants reject $50 and prefer the current $20 experience.
Evidence base is thin: regression skipped, competitor enrichment failed, and internal upgrade/churn/discount-usage data absent.
Financial exposure is low and within threshold, enabling a measured test.
conditions: Before broad rollout, revise or clarify the $20 discount cap, and test grandfathering or retention offers for existing $20 full-access merchants.
Add an in-app discount-usage meter and clear upgrade path so the $20 cap is forecastable rather than a surprise.
Stage rollout first to BFCM/promotional high-volume merchants who show strong $50 unlimited intent.
Run regression/entitlement testing for discount-limit enforcement and billing display before launch.
Validate the support occupancy assumption and pricing-query ticket baseline.
Define the $10,000 financial threshold and monitor upgrade/churn economics within the 4-month retention window.
dataLimitations: Regression status is skipped because no regression payload was provided; no pass/fail or coverage signal exists.
Market evidence is from Strategy C only and is limited by failed competitor enrichment, failed job-market queries, and absent install-base/overlap data.
Competitor pricing is from web snippets only; company_enrich failed for Rapi Bundles, Fast Bundles, and Kaching Bundles, and target-market company_search returned mostly agencies/app vendors.
Persona findings are from a synthetic 25-agent panel with 6–7 agents per segment; they are directional, not observed market behavior, and several distributions are polarized/bimodal.
No internal upgrade, churn, plan-mix, or discount-usage data was provided, so the share of $20 customers hitting the new cap cannot be estimated.
Financial CFO workspace scenario, memory, page, and integration calls returned validation errors; no detailed cost ledger or actual labor cost per engineer was provided.

Internal financial figures are self-reported, and LTV $40 vs 4-month retention at $8/merchant/month implies ~$32, a ~20% gap; financialThresholdAmount and expectedResourceConsumption lack definitions/units.
Feature document is named test-prd.txt and was not included in the raw bundle; persona document name is null.
